title: Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache
intro: A short, self-paced catch-up covering the essential lesson ideas. Check every question, then correct anything missed.

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Read the essential ideas and worked example before checking your understanding.

blocks.title: Why is memory needed?
blocks.text: Running programs need fast access to instructions and working data. Primary storage supports the CPU while programs run.

blocks.title: RAM
blocks.text: Random Access Memory stores programs and data currently in use. It is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is removed.

blocks.title: ROM
blocks.text: Read Only Memory is non-volatile and commonly stores firmware or start-up instructions.

blocks.title: Cache
blocks.text: CPU cache is small, very fast memory close to the processor holding frequently used data and instructions, reducing access time.

blocks.title: Visual model · Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache
blocks.caption: Different memory types serve different roles; saved files also need secondary storage.

blocks.title: Worked model · A laptop starts, opens a game, saves a level, then powers off. Explain what each type of memory does.
blocks.text: Non-volatile ROM/firmware supplies start-up instructions. The active operating system and game data are loaded into RAM from secondary storage. The processor can access frequently needed data faster from cache. Saving writes the level to non-volatile secondary storage; RAM contents are lost at power-off.

items: RAM — Volatile working memory for programs and data in use.
ROM — Non-volatile memory typically containing firmware.
cache — Small, very fast memory used by the CPU.
volatile — Loses stored contents when power is removed.

questions.feedback: RAM generally loses contents without power.

questions.prompt: Which type usually holds firmware or startup instructions?
questions.feedback: Non-volatile ROM or firmware storage holds start-up instructions.

options: Provides faster access to frequently used data
questions.answer: Provides faster access to frequently used data
questions.feedback: Cache is small and fast, reducing slower RAM accesses.

stages.label: Practise
stages.lead: Match, reorder and apply what you have learnt.

blocks.text: Consider power loss and what each type is designed to hold.

questions.prompt: Match the memory type to its main role.
questions.feedback: RAM is volatile working memory; ROM persists; cache speeds frequently needed access.

questions.prompt: Put a simple power-on and use sequence in order.
items: CPU uses RAM and cache while work runs
answer: CPU uses RAM and cache while work runs
questions.feedback: Boot firmware helps start the system, then working programs use RAM and cache.

questions.prompt: Which type loses stored information when power is removed?
questions.feedback: Volatile RAM cannot normally retain its contents without electricity.

questions.prompt: Where are unsaved changes to an open document generally held?
questions.feedback: Active data may be in RAM until explicitly saved to non-volatile storage.

questions.prompt: The starter program sets score = 10, then score = 15, then prints score. What is output?
questions.feedback: The second assignment replaces the working value with 15.

questions.prompt: If the second assignment becomes score = 20, what is output?
questions.feedback: The last assignment sets score to 20.

questions.prompt: Why might cache make a running program faster?
options: It holds frequently used data near the CPU
It keeps files when power is lost
It is larger than secondary storage
questions.answer: It holds frequently used data near the CPU
questions.feedback: Cache reduces access latency for frequently used values and instructions.
